newsitem.title: UK: Workers' stress creates big bill for UK firms -TUC.
newsitem.headline: Workers' stress creates big bill for UK firms -TUC.

text.p: Workplace stress costs Britain around six billion pounds ($9.9 billion) a year in sick leave and related charges but few managers appear aware of official guidelines to prevent pressure at work, a trades union group said on Friday.
"Stress has become the new workplace epidemic. But it is neither inevitable or acceptable," John Monks, secretary general secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), said at a union conference.
The TUC, an umbrella group for British unions, is urging the government to get tough on employers by ensuring they know their legal duties to protect their workforce.

In 1995, the government's Health and Safety Executive (HSE) produced a booklet 'Stress at Work - a guide for employers' but today's report revealed that only one in eight managers were even aware of the HSE guidelines.

The TUC's latest campaign comes as union leaders renew their drive to push employment issues up the political agenda after the Labour Party crushed the Conservatives at the May 1 election and a European Union Summit in Amsterdam this month made jobs a priority.
The TUC said it wanted a legally enforceable code of practice to "ensure employers know and meet their responsibilities" when it came to workers suffering from stress-related symptoms.

The report, compiled as a survey of 245 workers' views, found that respondents considered the following (in descending order) the main causes of anxiety at work -- time pressures and deadlines; work overload; threat of job losses; lack of consultation and communication with the organisation; and under staffing.
At the same time, over half those employees surveyed reported that management had taken no action to reduce workplace stress.
"Stress is often considered a sign of weakness or failure and a result many employees refuse to accept that they or other work colleagues can suffer from it," the unions' report concluded.

Greater awareness of the problem would be created through stress management programmes and other forms of education. Such schemes would also force management to acknowledge many of the pressures their workforce were subjected to, it said.
